title: REST API
griotIntro: At the great mosque of Touba, every door has a precise use known to all: entering, leaving, praying.
A REST API works the same way: each HTTP verb has a precise, predictable use on a resource.

explanation.text: The HTTP verb expresses the action to perform on a resource, not the URL — avoid URLs like `/getUserById`. A good API is also stateless (each request carries everything it needs, with no memory kept server-side) and returns the right status code. Click each line for details.
explanation.code:
GET    /users/42        // fetch user 42
POST   /users           // create a new user
PUT    /users/42        // fully replace user 42
PATCH  /users/42        // partially update user 42
DELETE /users/42        // delete user 42
HEAD   /users/42        // like GET but without a body: useful to check a resource exists
GET    /users?role=admin // filter a collection via query params, never via a new verb
PATCH  /users/42  { email: null }  // gotcha: null clears the field, a field absent from the JSON leaves it unchanged

annotations.note: Reads without ever modifying — a GET request must stay "safe": it can be called as many times as you want with no side effect.
Creates a new resource. NOT idempotent: two calls create two different users. Expected response: 201.
Replaces the resource ENTIRELY — an omitted field is erased. Idempotent: calling it again with the same data always yields the same final state.
Only modifies the fields provided, the rest stays unchanged. Unlike POST, PATCH is meant to be idempotent.
Deletes the resource. Idempotent in practice: deleting it a second time should break nothing, even if the response becomes 404.
HEAD returns the same headers as a GET but without the response body — handy to check a resource exists without downloading its whole content.
Filtering, sorting and pagination go through query parameters on the existing resource, never through a one-off endpoint or verb invented for the occasion.
Classic interview trap: in a PATCH, an explicit `null` value clears the field, while a field simply absent from the JSON is left untouched — make sure to distinguish the two on the backend.

timeline.label: HTTP Request
timeline.description: The client sends a request (e.g. GET /users/42) to the server.

timeline.label: Routing
timeline.description: The server identifies which route/controller should handle the request.

timeline.label: Processing
timeline.description: The business logic runs, possibly with a database access.

timeline.label: Response
timeline.description: The server returns an HTTP status code and data (often as JSON).

timeline.label: Client-side rendering
timeline.description: The frontend receives the response and updates the interface for the user.

useCases: The backend of this Teranga Code project itself: `POST /auth/register`, `GET /progress`, `POST /progress/xp` follow exactly these REST conventions.
A mobile app that consumes the same REST API as a website, without duplicating business logic server-side.
An order management system where `GET /orders/:id` fetches an order and `PATCH /orders/:id` updates only its status.

relatedTools.name: Express / NestJS / Fastify
relatedTools.description: The most widely used Node.js frameworks for building REST APIs, each with a different flexibility/structure trade-off.

relatedTools.name: Postman / Insomnia
relatedTools.description: Tools for manually testing REST endpoints without writing a frontend, indispensable in backend development.

relatedTools.name: Swagger / OpenAPI
relatedTools.description: A standard for documenting a REST API readably and automatically generating interactive documentation.

bugHunt.explanation: A GET request must never have a side effect (it must stay safe and idempotent) — the deletion should use the DELETE method, not GET.

practice.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
options: PUT replaces the entire resource, PATCH only modifies the fields provided
PUT and PATCH are interchangeable as long as the request body contains all fields
PATCH always requires an identifier in the request body, never in the URL

feedback.correct: Exactly — a very classic backend technical interview question.
feedback.incorrect: PUT = full replacement (an omitted field is erased). PATCH = partial update (fields not provided stay unchanged). That's the key distinction.

quiz.question: What does "stateless" mean for a REST API?
options: The server keeps no session state between two requests; each request carries everything it needs
The server can process requests in any order, regardless of their content
Each request must necessarily open a new TCP connection

quiz.question: A POST /users request successfully creates a new user. What status code should the response return?
A client sends the same DELETE /orders/17 request twice in a row (for example because a network issue caused a retry). If the API is well designed to be idempotent, what is the expected behavior?
options: The final state is the same after both calls: order 17 is deleted, regardless of whether one of the two calls returns 404 the second time
The second call must necessarily return a 500 error to signal the repetition
The second call deletes another order to compensate

quiz.question: What does status code 401 mean as opposed to 403?
options: 401 = not authenticated (not logged in), 403 = authenticated but not authorized (lacks permissions)
401 concerns client errors, 403 concerns server errors
401 and 403 are interchangeable depending on the backend framework used

quiz.question: In an interview, you're asked how to evolve a REST API already used by several mobile clients in production, if you need to change the response structure of GET /users/:id. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Introduce a new versioned endpoint (e.g. /api/v2/users/:id) and keep the old one running while clients migrate
Modify the existing endpoint directly: mobile clients will update automatically
Remove the old endpoint immediately to force the migration

quiz.question: To filter, sort or paginate a collection in REST (e.g. GET /users?role=admin&sort=name&page=2), what is the best practice?
options: Use query parameters on the existing GET endpoint, without changing the resource itself
Create a separate endpoint for every possible combination of filters
Send the filter criteria in the body of a GET request

quiz.question: Which HTTP header lets a client avoid re-downloading a resource that hasn't changed since its last call?
options: ETag, combined with If-None-Match on subsequent requests
Content-Type
Authorization

culture: REST isn't the only API culture: GraphQL (Facebook) and gRPC (Google) each have their communities convinced their approach is superior. REST remains dominant for its simplicity and universality, but the "REST vs GraphQL" debate comes up very often in architecture interviews.

pionnier.portrait: American computer scientist, co-author of the HTTP/1.1 specification and co-inventor of the Apache HTTP server.
pionnier.contribution: He defined the REST (Representational State Transfer) architecture in chapter 5 of his doctoral dissertation in 2000, at the University of California, Irvine.
pionnier.problematique: The web needed a clear architectural style for building distributed systems that remain scalable, simple and evolvable, as the number of applications communicating over HTTP was exploding.
pionnier.solution: He formalized a set of constraints (client-server, statelessness on the server side, uniform interface, layered system) describing how the web was already working with HTTP, rather than inventing a new protocol.
pionnier.resultat: REST became the dominant architectural style for web APIs, adopted today by nearly all online services, well before the more recent rise of GraphQL or gRPC.

ambiguite.question: Does a "RESTful" API always strictly follow REST?
ambiguite.reponse: Rarely 100%: REST as defined by Roy Fielding imposes strict constraints (HATEOAS in particular, almost never implemented). In practice, most "REST APIs" on the market only follow part of the constraints.

title: Databases: SQL vs NoSQL
griotIntro: The millet granary arranges every sack in a fixed, precise order; the market, on the other hand, organizes itself differently every day depending on what arrives.
SQL structures data according to a rigid schema; NoSQL adapts to more flexible or massive data.

explanation.text: SQL guarantees strict relationships and consistency (ACID); NoSQL sometimes sacrifices that rigor for schema flexibility or scalability. Click the lines to compare the two approaches.

annotations.note: We select columns coming from TWO different tables — typical of the relational model.
`JOIN` links two tables via a foreign key (`user_id`) — without it, there's no way to combine the two.
Here, the orders are directly nested inside the user document — no join needed, but the data is duplicated if the same item appears elsewhere.
An index speeds up reads by email but slows down every write, since the index also has to be updated — a very classic trade-off in relational databases.
This is the real hidden cost of NoSQL denormalization: read speed is paid for by a risk of desynchronization if the duplicated data isn't updated everywhere it appears.

useCases: PostgreSQL (used in this project via Prisma) for strongly relational data: users, XP, badges with clear constraints.
MongoDB for storing user profiles whose structure varies a lot (preferences, history) without a rigid schema.
Redis (key-value) for very fast caching or temporary data (sessions, counters) that don't need complex relationships.

relatedTools.name: Prisma (used in this project)
relatedTools.description: An ORM that simplifies access to PostgreSQL in JavaScript/TypeScript, with migrations and automatic typing.

relatedTools.name: MongoDB / Mongoose
relatedTools.description: The most widely used document-oriented NoSQL database in JavaScript, with Mongoose as a modeling layer.

relatedTools.name: Redis
relatedTools.description: An in-memory key-value store, extremely fast, used for caching, sessions or task queues.

lines: const query = `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`;
bugHunt.explanation: Directly concatenating user input into the SQL query opens a SQL injection vulnerability (e.g. a malicious email like `' OR '1'='1`). You should use parameterized queries (placeholders) or an ORM like Prisma, which automatically escapes values.

practice.question: In which case is a document-oriented NoSQL database particularly well suited?
options: When the data structure varies a lot from one record to another, or horizontal scalability is a priority
When you need strict ACID transactions on complex relationships
Never, SQL is always preferable

feedback.correct: Exactly — it's a real trade-off, not an absolute hierarchy between the two worlds.
feedback.incorrect: It's the opposite: for strict transactions and complex relationships, SQL is often still preferable.

quiz.question: What does the acronym ACID mean in databases?
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — transaction reliability guarantees
An alternative query language to SQL
A type of NoSQL database

quiz.question: What is an index in a database, and why use one?
options: A structure that speeds up searches on a column, at the cost of extra work on write
A full copy of the database
A type of join

quiz.question: What is the difference between a SQL join (JOIN) and nested data in a NoSQL document?
options: JOIN links separate tables at read time; NoSQL can store related data directly within the same document
JOIN and nested data always produce exactly the same result, regardless of the use case
NoSQL represents relationships only through joins, exactly like SQL

quiz.question: Why is horizontal scalability (adding servers) often simpler with certain NoSQL databases?
options: They are designed from the start to shard data across multiple machines
They always store less data than SQL databases
SQL can technically never be distributed across multiple servers

quiz.question: In an interview, which answer shows good maturity about the SQL vs NoSQL choice?
options: "It depends on the need: data structure, required consistency, volume and access pattern"
"NoSQL is always better, it's more modern"
"SQL is obsolete, nobody uses it anymore"

quiz.question: An application must handle transfers between bank accounts, where debiting one account and crediting another must succeed or fail together, never leaving an inconsistent state. Which type of database is best suited?
options: A SQL database with ACID transactions
A document-oriented NoSQL database, for its schema flexibility
A key-value store like Redis, for its speed

quiz.question: In a NoSQL document that nests orders directly inside the user document, what is the main risk if a product name needs to be corrected while it appears in hundreds of already-recorded orders?
options: The duplicated data must be updated everywhere it appears, or risk inconsistency if one place is forgotten
No risk: NoSQL automatically syncs all duplicated copies of a piece of data
The problem doesn't arise because NoSQL forbids data duplication

culture: The "SQL vs NoSQL war" of the 2010s (fueled by MongoDB's boom) has largely settled down: current culture favors pragmatism — use PostgreSQL by default, and NoSQL only for specific scalability or schema flexibility needs.

pionnier.portrait: British mathematician and computer scientist, researcher at IBM starting in the 1960s.
pionnier.contribution: In 1970 he published the founding paper of the relational model ("A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks"), the origin of SQL databases.
pionnier.problematique: Databases of the time organized data according to their physical storage implementation, which made applications fragile to the slightest change in internal structure.
pionnier.solution: He proposed representing data as tables (relations) manipulable through a relational algebra, independent of how they are physically stored.
pionnier.resultat: This model gave rise to the SQL language and to relational database management systems (RDBMS) like Oracle, PostgreSQL or MySQL, which remain the dominant standard for structured data almost 55 years later.

ambiguite.question: Is PostgreSQL purely a SQL database?
ambiguite.reponse: Not only: PostgreSQL natively supports JSON/JSONB columns, which lets it mimic certain NoSQL use cases while keeping ACID guarantees. The SQL/NoSQL boundary is blurrier than it was ten years ago.

title: Monolith vs microservices
griotIntro: One big family compound, or several small independent houses linked by the same paths: two ways of organizing a community.
A monolith bundles everything into a single application; microservices split each function into independent services.

explanation.text: A monolith is simple to develop and deploy at first, but couples everything together at scale. Microservices decouple, at the cost of much greater operational complexity.

annotations.note: All routes run in the same process, deployed together — a bug in `payments` can crash the whole service, including `users`.
A single deployment for the whole app: simple to develop at first, but everything is coupled.
Each service runs on its own port, potentially its own database and its own team — independently deployable and scalable, at the cost of real network complexity.
The modular monolith keeps a single deployment (so simpler to operate) while enforcing clear boundaries between modules — often a good intermediate step before truly splitting into microservices.
The API Gateway is the single client-facing entry point: it routes to the right microservice, handles centralized authentication, and spares the frontend from needing to know each service's address.

useCases: This project's backend (`backend/`) is a simple monolith: a single Express server bundling auth and progress, suited to its current size.
Netflix or Amazon use microservices at large scale: the payment service can be deployed and scaled independently of the recommendation service.
A startup that starts with a monolith, then extracts the payment service into a separate microservice when it becomes a bottleneck.

relatedTools.name: Kubernetes
relatedTools.description: The standard for orchestrating many microservices in production (deployment, scaling, resilience).

relatedTools.name: RabbitMQ / Kafka
relatedTools.description: Message queues that let microservices communicate asynchronously and in a decoupled way.

relatedTools.name: Docker Compose (used in this project)
relatedTools.description: A good starting point to orchestrate a few related services locally, before you need Kubernetes.

lines: const order = await db.orders.findUnique({ where: { id: orderId } });
const user = await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id: order.userId } });
bugHunt.explanation: A microservice must never access another service's database directly — this recreates the strong coupling typical of a "distributed monolith". The right approach is to call the API (REST/gRPC) exposed by users-service to fetch user data.

practice.question: For a small team starting a new product, which architecture is generally recommended first?
options: A well-structured monolith, simpler and faster to develop
Microservices from day one, regardless of context
Neither, you should always go serverless

feedback.correct: Exactly — a very common piece of interview advice: "start with a monolith, split it if/when the need appears".
feedback.incorrect: Microservices add real operational complexity, rarely justified at the very start of a project.

quiz.question: What is the main drawback of microservices compared to a monolith?
options: Increased operational complexity: networking, distributed data consistency, observability
They are always cheaper to host, regardless of traffic
They cannot be containerized

quiz.question: What is a "single point of failure" in a poorly designed monolith?
options: A component whose failure brings down the entire application
A place in the code with only one function
A type of database

quiz.question: How do microservices generally communicate with each other?
options: Via network calls (REST API, gRPC) or message queues
Only by sharing the same memory
They always share the same database to stay in sync

quiz.question: What is a sign that a monolith should consider splitting up?
options: Several teams keep stepping on each other in the same code, or one component has very different scalability needs from the rest
The project has fewer than 100 lines of code
Only when the team exceeds 50 developers, never before

quiz.question: What is a "modular monolith"?
options: A monolith organized into well-separated modules (clear boundaries), making a future split into microservices easier if needed
A strict synonym for microservices
An architecture that doesn't exist in practice

quiz.question: What is a clear signal that you should NOT migrate to microservices right away?
options: The team is small (2-3 developers) and the product hasn't found its market yet
A separate team has owned each business domain for over a year
One specific component has very different scalability needs from the rest of the system

quiz.question: In a microservices architecture, how do you guarantee the consistency of an operation spanning several services (e.g. order + payment + stock) when no global ACID transaction is possible?
options: The Saga pattern: a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action in case of failure
A classic SQL transaction shared directly across all services
It can't be managed: you must necessarily go back to a monolith

culture: Microservices had a strong hype effect in 2015-2020; current culture is more nuanced, with a movement back toward "modular monoliths" at some companies (including well-publicized cases like Amazon Prime Video).

pionnier.portrait: Software engineer, former Chief Cloud Architect at Netflix between 2007 and 2013.
pionnier.contribution: He led Netflix's migration from a monolith hosted in its own data centers to a microservices architecture deployed on AWS, and spoke extensively in public about the experience.
pionnier.problematique: Netflix had to absorb massive, fast-growing streaming traffic, while its monolithic architecture made deployments slow and fragile: a failure in one part of the system could bring down the whole site.
pionnier.solution: Split the application into independent services, each responsible for a specific business domain (billing, recommendations, video playback...), independently deployable and scalable, with a strong resilience culture (including the Chaos Monkey tool).
pionnier.resultat: This migration, completed around 2012, greatly helped popularize microservices architecture across the industry and let Netflix sustain its global growth without rethinking its architecture at every step.

ambiguite.question: Does having several services mean you have microservices?
ambiguite.reponse: Not necessarily: splitting an application into several services only makes them microservices if they are truly independent (deployment, database, team). Services sharing the same database are more of a distributed monolith.

title: Scalability & caching
griotIntro: A single bissap vendor can serve ten customers; to serve a thousand, you need several vendors and a system to spread the crowd.
Scalability is exactly that: preparing your system to absorb much more load without collapsing.

explanation.text: Caching reduces load by avoiding recomputing or re-querying what has already been requested recently — a topic much expected in system design interviews. Click the lines to see the cache-aside pattern.

annotations.note: We first check whether the data is already cached — a Redis access is much faster than a database query.
Cache found ("cache hit"): we return directly, without ever touching the database.
Cache missed ("cache miss"): we go fetch the data at its source, the database — slower.
We store the result in the cache for next time, with a 60s expiration (`EX 60`) — avoids serving stale data indefinitely.

Actively invalidating the key at write time (rather than waiting for the TTL) guarantees the next read will fetch fresh data from the database — a strategy that complements the TTL, not a replacement for it.

useCases: A CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront) that caches images and static files close to the user to reduce latency.
A load balancer in front of several instances of the same Node.js server during a traffic spike (e.g. a promotion launch).
Caching the result of a costly ranking (leaderboard) query so it's only recomputed once a minute instead of on every visit.

relatedTools.name: Redis
relatedTools.description: The most common choice for implementing a fast application cache in front of a slower database.

relatedTools.name: Cloudflare / CloudFront (CDN)
relatedTools.description: Content delivery networks that cache static files and pages close to the end user.

relatedTools.name: Nginx / HAProxy
relatedTools.description: Load balancers that distribute traffic across several instances of a server.

lines: const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: req.user.id } });
bugHunt.explanation: The cache key 'user-profile' is fixed and shared by every user: the first user who triggers a cache miss will have their profile cached and then served to ALL other users afterward. A per-user key is needed (e.g. `user-profile:${req.user.id}`), and ideally a TTL to avoid serving stale data indefinitely.

practice.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scalability?
options: Vertical = increasing the power of a single machine; horizontal = adding several machines
Vertical = adding several machines; horizontal = increasing the power of a single machine
Horizontal scalability only concerns the frontend

feedback.correct: Exactly — and horizontal scalability is generally preferred at large scale, despite its complexity.
feedback.incorrect: Vertical = a bigger machine. Horizontal = more machines. That's the fundamental distinction.

quiz.question: What is a load balancer for?
options: Distributing incoming requests across several servers to prevent any single one from being overloaded
Storing cached data
Compiling code in production

quiz.question: Why must a service be "stateless" to properly benefit from horizontal scalability?
options: Any instance can handle any request without depending on locally stored state
A stateless service always consumes less memory
It isn't a necessary condition

quiz.question: What is the main risk of using a cache?
options: Serving stale data if cache invalidation isn't well managed
A cache always doubles the disk space needed server-side
A cache can never expire

quiz.question: What is database replication?
options: Duplicating data across several servers for availability and to spread read load
Automatically removing duplicates
Encrypting the database

quiz.question: In a high-load system, why cache the result of a costly query rather than rerunning it every time?
options: To reduce load on the database and improve response time
Caching has no measurable effect on performance
Because the database can only be queried once

quiz.question: Which strategy keeps the cache in sync as soon as data changes in the database, without waiting for the TTL to expire?
options: Explicitly invalidate (delete) the cache key at the very moment the data is modified in the database
Always wait for the TTL to expire, regardless of the freshness needed
Completely disable the cache as soon as a piece of data might ever change

quiz.question: A heavily accessed cache key (e.g. a leaderboard) expires, and thousands of requests arrive at the same instant. What problem can this cause, and how can it be avoided?
options: A "cache stampede": all requests hit the database at once; it can be avoided with a lock or by regenerating the cache before it expires
No problem: Redis automatically balances the load with no special configuration
The cache for that key must be permanently removed to avoid the problem

culture: "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things" is a cult quote (Phil Karlton) that every backend developer runs into sooner or later.

pionnier.portrait: American developer, creator of the community site LiveJournal in the late 1990s.
pionnier.contribution: He created memcached in 2003 to speed up LiveJournal, an in-memory key-value caching system that has since become an industry standard and the direct origin of tools like Redis.
pionnier.problematique: LiveJournal, one of the biggest community sites of its time, saw its database saturated by millions of repeated read requests, which severely slowed down the site under heavy load.
pionnier.solution: Store the results of already-computed costly queries in RAM, on a cluster of dedicated servers, to serve them instantly on subsequent requests rather than going back to the database every time.
pionnier.resultat: Memcached was later adopted by web giants like Facebook, Wikipedia or YouTube to absorb massive traffic; Facebook publicly documented in 2013 (in the paper "Scaling Memcache at Facebook") how it ran thousands of memcached servers to serve billions of requests per second.

ambiguite.question: Does a cache always expire at the right time?
ambiguite.reponse: No, that's the classic trap: a TTL that's too long serves stale data, a TTL that's too short cancels the benefits of caching. There's no universal right answer, only a trade-off to tune based on the actual change frequency of the data.
